title: Chapter 118 — The Quadrant
paragraphs: The season for the equator at length drew near; and every day when Ahab, coming from his cabin, cast his eyes aloft, the vigilant helmsman would ostentatiously handle his spokes, and the eager sailors would quickly run to the braces and stand there with all their eyes fixed on the nailed doubloon — imagining that the long-wished-for command to point her prow for the equator would soon be given.

Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are like floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; clouds there are none; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is as the insufferable splendors of God's throne. Well may that eye of his be in it, for how can we bear to look at it? One morning, Ahab raised his ivory leg, steadied his body with his free knee against the boat's side, and taking from the binnacle the quadrant, began fixing it for observation.

Then gazing at his quadrant, and handling, one after another, its numerous mystical devices, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Baby's plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what after all can you do, but tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be? You can not tell where one single drop of water or one single grain of sand will be tomorrow noon. Curse you, you vain toy — and cursed be all things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose vivid vastness but scorches him! Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck — "no longer will I guide my earthly way by you. This world steers its own course and I am steering mine!"

As the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live and dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself — these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee's face. Unobserved he rose and glided away; while, awestruck by the spectacle of their commander, the sailors gathered together on the forecastle.

In an instant the yards swung round; and as the ship half-wheeled upon her heel, her three firm-seated graceful masts, erectly poised upon her long, ribbed hull, seemed as three acrobats pirouetting on one sufficient steed.
Standing between the bow-timbers, Starbuck watched the Pequod's tumultuous way, and Ahab's also, as he went lurching along the deck.

"I have sat before the dense coal fire and watched it all aglow, full of its tormented flaming life; and I have seen it wane at last, down, down, to dumbest dust. Old man of oceans! Of all this fiery life of yours, what will at length remain but one little heap of ashes!"

"Aye," cried Stubb, "but sea-coal ashes — mind you that, Mr. Starbuck — sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab mutter, 'Here someone thrusts these cards into these old hands of mine; swears that I must play them, and no others.' And damn me, Ahab, but you act right; live in the game, and die in it!"
